title: degraded-mode-routing-and-model-families
content:
Purpose and context

This is a working note describing an operational pattern we call \"degraded-mode routing\" — a control-plane-led approach to keep customer-facing inference APIs available when one or more capacity domains (region, tier, model family) are impaired. Focus is on model-variant downgrade, tiered capacity steering, and cross-region spillover. Goal: keep p99 latency within SLOs for high-tier customers while minimizing cost and quality regressions for others.

Problem space (why we need this)
- Capacity incidents will happen (partial GPU failures, regional routable networking issues, sudden traffic spikes).
- Blindly rejecting traffic or globally throttling is unacceptable for paid customers with SLAs.
- Running highest-quality models for all requests during overload is costly and increases latency.
- Model variants (quantized, small family members, distillations) provide different cost/latency/quality points we can leverage.

Design principles
1) Policy-first: Keep control logic declarative and versioned in the control plane; runtime applies small, well-tested core agents.
2) Graceful downgrade hierarchy: prefer lower-quality model variants before dropping requests.
3) Per-tenant SLO awareness: routing decisions must be weighted by customer tier and SLA.
4) Soft affinity and capacity-awareness: prefer local region and pinned capacity, only spillover when beneficial.
5) Observability + safety: every downgrade is annotated, sampled outputs are stored for quality monitoring and automated rollback if regressions are detected.

Key components (overview)
- Control plane policy store: JSON/YAML policies that encode preference lists (region, model-family, variant, tier) with versioning and rollout windows.
- Router agents (edge proxies): consult local cache of policies and telemetry (capacity tokens, health states) and enforce decision logic.
- Capacity telemetry: region/tier-level tokens emitted by serving runtime (free GPU slots, tail latency, queue depth).
- Fallback catalogue: per-model-family list of compatible variants and transformation adapters (e.g., tokenization/format shim).
- Circuit breakers / slow-start: per-tenant and per-route breakers that trigger degraded-mode decisions.

Degraded-mode state machine (simplified)
1) NORMAL: preferred model + local region, no degradation.
2) CONGESTED: queue depth / token threshold exceeded; router checks policy -> attempt local model variant with smaller memory footprint (quantized) and reduced max_length.
3) DEGRADED_SPILLOVER: local region saturated and remote region has spare capacity; initiate soft spillover with sticky session window (30s) and observe success ratio.
4) PARTIAL_REJECT: all variants and spillover saturated; apply per-tenant rate-shaping and return structured retry-info (Retry-After, suggested cheaper model).
5) FAIL_OPEN/ESCALATE: emergency mode for highest-tier customers: fall back to best-effort synchronous alternatives (cached completions, fast embedding fallback) and page on-call.

Policy model (how we express routing rules)
- Example policy fields (flattened representation for this doc):
  - route_id: text_generate.v1
  - priority_classes: [enterprise, standard, free]
  - regional_preference: [closest, soft_affinity, global]
  - model_family: [redwood-llama-70b, redwood-llama-13b]
  - variant_order: [fp16, int8, distill-7b]
  - spillover_thresholds: {cpu_queue: 75%, gpu_free: 8}  <-- runtime interprets these
  - max_spillover_per_minute: 120
  - telemetry_window_seconds: 10

(We keep human-readable names in the policy, runtime does the mapping to concrete instance pools.)

Model-variant compatibility and adapters
- Not all fallbacks are drop-in. We maintain a small set of adapters that handle expected differences (context length, tokenizer differences, reply format). Example: for a family downgrade from 70B -> 13B: shrink max_context from 4096 -> 2048, enable forced-summarize pre-step for long prompts, map function-calling hooks to a compatible subset.
- Catalog entries include: model_hash, family_tag, supported_max_tokens, quantized_flag, known-quality-delta (cheap metric from eval harness).

Capacity steering and tokens (runtime signal)
- Serving processes export token budgets (free_slots, soft_limit_pct, mean_inflight) per pool. The control plane aggregates into a regional view.
- Router applies a simple token-bucket: if remote_region.free_slots > spillover_min AND route_spillover_count < max_spillover_per_minute -> allow spillover for up to X% of requests for that route class.

Per-tenant shaping and fairness
- Each tenant has a tier (enterprise/standard/free) with SLO weights. On saturation we apply a weighted shaping algorithm: enterprise keep 90% of pre-degrade capacity, standard 60%, free 20%. Shapes are applied at the edge router, not at backend.

Observability and quality guardrails
- Every downgraded request is tagged with: original_model, chosen_variant, reason_code, control_plane_policy_version, spillover_region.
- Sampled responses (1% baseline, up to 10% when in degraded mode) are shipped to the eval pipeline with a tag so we can run automated quality checks (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity to baseline).
- If quality delta > threshold for 5m window, automatic rollback of that specific policy version and open a P0 ticket.

Operator tooling and runbooks (TL;DR)
- UI: Policy diff view (policy version vs active), live capacity heatmap, spillover counters, tenant-level impact view.
- Quick actions: force-route-to-region, disable-variant, increase spillover-rate, emergency-throttle-tenant.
- Runbook snippets: when region X shows >85% queue: 1) check QPS/allocations, 2) enable distill variant for standard/free, 3) open incident bridge, 4) verify sampled quality and watch rollback threshold.

Examples (concrete scenarios)
1) Regional maintenance (planned): we mark region as 'drain' for 10m windows, policy soft-affinity->global, warm-up remote pools by pre-warming 10% baseline via controlled spillover to avoid cold-start penalty.
2) Sudden traffic spike (unplanned): circuit breaker trips for standard and free -> standard falls back to int8 variants, free gets 429 with Retry-After and suggestion to try embeddings-only flow. Enterprise customers are routed to remote region using synchronous spillover and paged to on-call if tail latency > 2x SLO.
3) GPU OOM pattern on new model load: auto-fallback to smaller model family and pin a reduced max_tokens. Alert generated and rollout blocked (control plane prevents new policy promotions for 30m).

Testing and validation plan
- Unit tests for policy interpreter (edge cases: missing variants, incompatible adapter).
- Integration sim harness: synthesize region-level tokens and run a 1h adversarial sequence (sudden spike, slow burn) and verify policy invariants (no more than configured spillover, no silent quality regression).
- Chaos testing: kill a regional control agent and observe that router agents fallback to cached policies and continue to enforce shaping.

Open questions and TODOs
- How aggressive should auto-rollbacks be for small but noisy quality deltas (false positives from stochastic output)? Need to tune sample sizes.
- Should we allow user-configurable degradation preferences (e.g., customer opts-in to cheaper models to reduce cost)? Privacy and billing implications to clarify.
- Metrics contract: define a compact, efficient telemetry proto for token budgets (proposal attached in linked_confluence).

Appendix: sample policy snippet (human-readable)
route: text.generate.chat.v1
priority:
  - enterprise
  - standard
  - free
regional_preference: soft_affinity
model_family_preferences:
  - family: redwood-lift-70b
    variants: [fp16, int8]
    fallback_adapters: [context-trim, summarize-pre]
  - family: redwood-lift-13b
    variants: [fp16, int8, distill-13b]
spillover:
  global_threshold_pct: 85
  max_spillover_per_min: 60
  warmup_percent: 10

Notes-to-self: keep this as minimal and actionable policy syntax; we can expand to a full schema later. Reach out to @samir in #platform-routing for recent instrumentation changes.

End of doc.
